name: Interview market making, set 3
description: Market-making questions: cards revealed, Fermi errors, intervals, calibration, moving the centre, a ledger, hedging and thinking aloud. Each item keeps its own schedule.

items.prose: Four cards are dealt face down from one shuffled deck. A contract pays £10 for each heart among the four. The first two cards are turned over: a heart and a club.
items.question: What is the fair value of the contract now, in pounds?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add the shown heart to two hidden cards, each a heart with chance 12/50.

byKey.fresh-deck: You gave each hidden card a 13/52 chance. Two cards are out, one a heart, so each is a heart with chance 12/50.
byKey.one-out: You took only the heart out of the deck. The club is out too, so 12 hearts sit among 50 cards.
byKey.before-reveal: You priced the contract before the reveals. The shown heart is now certain, worth £10 on its own.
byKey.dropped-shown: You left out the heart already shown. It pays £10 for sure.

explain.text: The shown heart pays £10 for sure, and the club pays nothing. Each of the two hidden cards is a heart with chance 12/50 = 0.24. So the value is 10 + 2 × 10 × 0.24 = £14.80.

items.prose: You estimate the dentists in a town as yearly visits divided by the visits one dentist handles a year. Later you learn your visits-per-dentist figure was half the true value. Every other input was right.
items.question: What does that do to your estimate?

options.why: You treated the input as a multiplier. It divides, so a figure that is too small makes the answer too big.

options.text: It is four times too high.
options.why: You squared the error. One input off by a factor of 2 moves the answer by a factor of 2.

options.text: Hardly anything, since errors cancel out.
options.why: Errors cancel only when inputs are off in opposite directions. Here only one input is off.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask whether the faulty input multiplies or divides.

explain.text: The estimate is the visits divided by the visits per dentist. Halving the divisor doubles the answer. So the estimate is twice the true count.

items.prose: A fair coin will be flipped 100 times. The interviewer wants an interval for the count of heads, centred on 50, holding at least 95%.
items.question: Which of these intervals, centred on 50, is the tightest that holds at least 95%?

options.why: That is one standard deviation each side and holds only about 73%.
You were close, but it holds 94.3%, just short of 95%.
It holds 99.8%, wider than you need. A tighter interval still reaches 95%.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Use mean 50 and standard deviation 5, then check the ends.

explain.text: The count has mean 50 and standard deviation $\sqrt{100 \times 0.25} = 5$, so centre the interval on 50. Two standard deviations each side gives 40 to 60, which holds 96.5% exactly. Dropping one count at each end, 41 to 59, falls to 94.3%.

items.prose: In a practice week you gave 20 intervals, each meant to hold the answer 80% of the time. Only 12 held it.
items.question: What should you change?

options.text: Widen your intervals: 12 of 20 is 60%, far below 80%.
Narrow them: missing shows you are too cautious.
options.why: Misses mean your intervals were too narrow. Narrowing makes them miss more.

options.text: Nothing: 12 of 20 is close to 16 of 20.
options.why: A well-calibrated 80% quoter holds 12 or fewer only about 3% of the time.

options.text: Keep the width and move each centre up.
options.why: Nothing says your misses fell on one side. The hit rate says the width is wrong.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare your hit rate with the 80% you aimed for.

explain.text: At 80% you expect 16 hits in 20. A well-calibrated quoter holds 12 or fewer with chance about 0.032. So your intervals are too narrow: widen them until about 16 in 20 hold.

items.prose: Your fair value is 50. A customer sells you 5 lots at your bid, and you move your fair value to 49.4. You move by the same amount for every lot traded.
items.question: Another customer sells you 3 lots. What is your new fair value?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the move per lot from the first trade.

byKey.same-move: You moved 0.6 again. That move was for 5 lots; 3 lots move 3 × 0.12 = 0.36.
byKey.moved-up: You moved up. A customer selling to you hints the value is lower, so move down.

explain.text: The first trade moved you 0.6 for 5 lots, which is 0.12 a lot. Three more lots move you 3 × 0.12 = 0.36. So the new fair value is 49.4 − 0.36 = 49.04.

items.prose: You trade one contract, starting flat. In order you buy 3 at 42, sell 5 at 45 and buy 4 at 41. Then you sell 2 at 46 and buy 1 at 44. The contract is now marked at 43.
items.question: What is your P&L at the mark?

widget.accept: 26: cash of −17 plus a long position of 1 marked at 43.
widget.label: P&L

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Mark each trade at 43, or add the cash to the open position at 43.

byKey.cash-only: You counted the cash only. You are still long 1, worth 43 at the mark.
byKey.dropped-loser: You left out the last buy at 44. Marked at 43, it loses 1.

explain.text: Each trade at the mark: +3, +10, +8, +6 and −1, which totals 26. Cash is −126 + 225 − 164 + 92 − 44 = −17, and the long 1 at 43 brings it to 26. The only losing trade was the last buy at 44.

items.prose: You are long 5 baskets. Each basket gains £2.40 for every point the index rises. A hedge contract gains £0.80 for every point.
items.question: How many hedge contracts do you sell to be flat to the index?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide your total exposure per point by the hedge's exposure per point.

byKey.one-basket: You hedged one basket. You hold 5, so sell 5 × 3.
byKey.multiplied: You multiplied by 0.80. Divide your exposure by the hedge's £0.80 a point.

explain.text: Your exposure is 5 × £2.40 = £12 a point. Each hedge contract covers £0.80 a point. So sell 12/0.80 = 15 contracts.

items.prose: The interviewer says: "Make me a market in the number of letters in your name, times 7."
items.question: What do you say first?

options.text: Ask which name counts, first or full. Then say you know the value, so you quote very tight around it.
Quote a wide market, say 20 at 60, since names vary in length.
options.why: You priced it as if you did not know. It is your own name, so you know the value.

options.text: Count silently, then say the number with no bid or offer.
options.why: You gave a number, not a market. Say your reasoning, then quote a bid and an offer.

options.text: Refuse to quote, since the interviewer may know the answer from your CV.
options.why: Refusing scores nothing. Both sides may know it, which is why the quote should be tight.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask what you already know about the number.

explain.text: The value is fixed and you know it, once you agree which name counts. A wide market invites a trade at a price you know is wrong. Saying the question back, then quoting tight, shows you noticed what you know.
